articles.title: “FROM THE TIME I CAME IN …”
articles.author: A. B. Parker
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: I think we were made aware of a challenge on Lord’s day as to whether we have the consciousness of the Lord coming to us as we are together for the Supper; whether we come together to partake of the Supper in active faith; that we believe that the Lord will come to us.
There are two sides—one is His coming, the other is our apprehension or experience of it. I have thought for a long time that the scripture read is outstandingly related to this exercise.

The Lord said to Simon, “I entered into thy house”, and then He said what Simon did not do. It may be that the Lord Jesus comes and we do not do anything in the way of deep, inward, appreciative recognition of His coming. It is a challenge as to how fully, how deeply, we get into the matter. True inward experiences at the Supper represent real, vital christianity.

We may have a clear ritual and respond to the Lord Jesus, known as God over all, blessed for ever, become Man, having accomplished the mighty work of redemption, having been raised from the dead and glorified; we may speak to Him about this; we may speak to Him of our links with Him as His brethren, and speak to Him of union; we may respond to the blessed Spirit, approach the Father, and worship God. This all can be done as understanding what is right in ritual, but we may not have the inward consciousness of the Lord having come to us or of His leadership—it is possible. I am not saying that we do not get beyond ritual. The question should be raised in each heart as to what extent we really find ourselves affected inwardly.

What is spiritual is greater than what is physical, or natural. Daniel, for instance, when, the heavenly messenger spoke to him, was without strength, he could not rise up, he needed to be strengthened; the spiritual had that effect on the physical. The apostle John, on the isle of Patmos, saw the Lord in His judicial form and attitude as He walked in the midst of the seven golden lamps, and he fell at His feet as dead. Do we have any experience, inwardly, from having to do with the Lord as having come amongst us? Flesh and blood are incapable of sustaining what is spiritual, except as the blessed Spirit helps us. He will help us to get into the spiritual realm and engage in what is spiritual as we move under the leadership of Christ.

These things are very real, and I have been much concerned that I do not experience, as deeply as I would, the inward feelings which are moved by having to do with the Lord, personally, and having to do with the Holy Spirit as, being strengthened by Him in the inner man. Hence, I often call upon the Spirit to quicken me and help me in my affections to be rightly in the meeting, because the Lord is looking for a real response from hearts really committed and devoted.

This woman at the feet of Jesus had, no doubt, come there because of a conscious, felt need. We do not come together with a bad conscience. At least, we should not do so, for provision has been made that we should not. But it is a fact that the Lord has not yet come for us, and conditions in the world, in christendom, and in our own hearts, too, need to be overcome. We certainly need to prove ourselves and so eat, being conscious of the holiness of the things in which we engage. The Spirit helps us in this. This woman may have been affected by her need and her state. I believe that the alabaster box is an indication that this was so, for as helped by the Spirit of God, no doubt, to distinguish between good and evil her appreciation of Christ, represented in the myrrh, would be protected in the alabaster box from taint or pollution from circumstances in which she had moved. Indeed, she herself was like the alabaster box. In her inward soul her love for Christ would cause her to shrink from everything which might taint that precious appreciation of the One who had come to meet her need. She washed His feet, she wiped His feet with the hair of her head, she kissed His feet and anointed them with myrrh.

The Lord, in speaking of what she had done, quickly reaches the point of His coming in. He relates it to her kisses—“She from the time I came in has not ceased kissing my feet”. I have the sense, dear brethren, that this woman, having come to Jesus because of a felt need, was changed in her feelings at the feet of Jesus. As she washed His feet she became wholly absorbed with the Person, forgetting self. The footnote says, ‘ardently kissed’. This is what we want to reach in response to Christ! Naturally, our minds are frivolous, wandering; in the midst of the most precious matters they go off at a tangent. But this woman was absolutely absorbed with the preciousness of Christ. The Lord said, “She from the time I came in has not ceased kissing my feet”. I believe it was at that time when her sense of need disappeared and Christ filled her heart. He did not refer to the time He came through Simon’s door, I am sure. It was the moment when He got full entrance into the woman’s heart. This, I believe, is how the Lord comes in. He wanted to get into Simon’s heart, too, but we have no evidence that He ever did.

It is a challenge to us as to what our feelings are as we are together. Are we prepared to give the Lord some refreshment as He comes? Does He find us engaged with thoughts of Himself? Are we on the tip-toe of expectancy? Are we alert to discern His movements in leadership?

And does what we know give place to what we feel? This is an area of things in which the Lord would help us, for the service of God, in its vital character, depends upon our discernment of how and where the Lord will lead us. It may well be that the Lord has raised the challenge with us because He is looking for greater depth of feeling and response to Himself, giving Him liberty to impart to us some fresh touch when, in union, we become one with Him in His feelings and desires, coming under His leadership in access to the Father through Him and by one Spirit.

It was just these few thoughts, dear brethren, relating to the Lord coming in amongst us, that I felt free to suggest, to encourage us to become wholly absorbed with Christ and available to Him for the service of praise. May we be helped in them for His satisfaction as well as for our own blessing.
In one of our earlier readings we referred to Paul’s salutation to “the brethren all”, (2

Timothy 4: 21), and the question arises. Who are “the brethren all”? Earlier in the epistle he had said, “All who are in Asia … have turned away from me”, 2 Timothy 1: 15. He also spoke of certain individuals going to certain places, one of them having loved the present age (2 Timothy 4: 10). It is not suggested that Demas and those that had forsaken Paul were not still christians, but the question arises, Could they be included in “the brethren all”? I would think not. The term ‘brethren’ is very loosely used, and we have ourselves to acknowledge that we often use it loosely; but in the Scriptures it is used carefully. We must learn, dear brethren, to distinguish between things that differ. For example, Scripture speaks of believers; it speaks of disciples, and it speaks of brethren, and we must learn to distinguish.
In the life of Jesus it is said that certain believed on Him because of the signs He did, but Jesus did not trust Himself to them, because He knew what was in them (John 2: 23–25).

Therefore it is an exercise to us as to whether, at the end of the days, we can rightly be called brethren. How easy it is to take that name! From the divine standpoint, of course, we would recognise that it would apply to the saints, but it is a great exercise as to whether we practically conform to that name as true in the last days to the ministry of Paul. When he sent that salutation I think he would have in his mind persons who were characteristically true, here in the testimony, and this would raise an exercise with every one of us. Paul was a faithful man and the effect of his ministry would be to produce faithfulness in us. I believe the Lord would help us in this direction. He does not raise these questions with us to condemn us for our weakness, but rather to encourage us to open our souls to the Holy Spirit that we might be formed in the characteristics proper to brethren.

Now having this in mind, I read these three scriptures. One of the first things Saul heard was, “Brother”. Evidently he was a praying man. The Lord said, “Behold, he is praying”. How essential this is for all of us! I feel for myself that these simple devotions that christians should have are inclined to drop out of my experience. The Lord would have us to be dependent. A praying man shows two things, I think—one is that he is dependent upon God, and recognises his need; and the other is that he has confidence in God to meet it. May the Lord keep us in dependence and confidence. Saul had been very independent; a great man among the Jews. I expect he had said his prayers, and maybe we do, but the Lord noted now, “Behold, he is praying”. I believe he was brought into dependence.

Now Ananias goes to him and says, “Saul, brother”—What a greeting!—“The Lord has sent me, Jesus that appeared to thee in the way in which thou camest, that thou mightest see”. This shows how quickly a person can be regarded as a brother. He would, no doubt, grow in it.

You think of the man on the Damascus road. Was he brotherly? You could hardly think of him as such, and yet now the Lord has so worked with him that he is a subject man, and can be called a brother. I would love to be addressed like this, dear brethren. If I were to say to you, as John did, “I John, your brother” (Revelation 1: 9), you might say to me—or those that know me well might say to me—‘Then you had better be a little more brotherly’. The fact is that these men, such as Paul, and John, displayed the spirit of a brother. Another man is called “the beloved brother and faithful minister”, in that order (Colossians 4: 7). The order should be noticed. How great it is to be able to be addressed as a “beloved brother”. I receive letters addressed like that, and I ask the Lord, Am I?—and even a letter like that becomes an exercise. May we all be exercised about this, because this is individual, “Saul, brother”.

Now in the second passage there is a circle sitting around Jesus, and you will notice that His mother and His brethren were seeking Him. Some say to Him, “Behold, thy mother and thy brethren seek thee without”. They would claim Him on natural lines. Jesus says, “Who is my mother or my brethren?”. Then He looks around in a circuit. I think the Lord would look around in a circuit here. These words must have been very searching to them, as to us—“For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and sister, and mother”. This aspect of the brethren relates to those who are faithful to the will of God. The heavenly side is in John 20, relationships with Him as the ascended Man, but in this chapter it is the moral side, as we call it, that is, persons here who are true, who do the will of God. You can see how such are related to Him because He came to do the will of God, “Lo, I come … to do,
O God, thy will” (Hebrews 10; 7), and God’s will governed Him throughout the whole of His life, even unto death.

Now the Lord would raise a question with us, as, to whether we are related to Him morally in this way, or whether we may seek Him and make claims on other ground. A little earlier (Mark 3: 21) it says, “And his relatives having heard of it went out to lay hold on him, for they said, He is out of his mind”, and now you find them seeking Him on natural lines. The Lord does not allow this; He says, “Whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and sister, and mother”. This shows, dear brethren, that one individual can do it. Nevertheless, He looks around in a circuit and says, “Behold my mother and my brethren”, showing that while I am to be exercised personally to be a brother, in this sense, yet I am to come into a circle called His brethren. Now He would raise the question in these days, I believe, “Who is my mother or my brethren?”. Is there a circuit around which He can look and say, “My mother and my brethren”? I believe there is, dear brethren, and the Lord would exercise us to find that circuit. A circuit has a centre, and the Centre is Christ. Christ is everything and in each one. How wonderful to find a circle faithful to the truth in a dark day! May the Lord help us to find it, and remain in it, faithful to Him in these days.

Now in John 20 we have a rather different aspect. Here, again, they are His own words, “Go to my brethren and say to them, I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. How wonderful that He should regard them like this!—persons of His order, associated with Him above, knowing His Father as their Father, and His God as their God. What a message! How we would love to receive that message. But I believe, dear brethren, that if we are to enter practically into the privilege of being His brethren above, we must be faithful as His brethren here, doing the will of God. You can see from this the great need not only of grasping the truth objectively, but of being exercised that there should be a subjective answer to it.

Now Mary gets this message and she comes bringing word to the disciples that “she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her”. Now note, she brings word to the disciples—followers, those who are true to Him, as we were reminded earlier, those who persevered with Him in His temptations. Note also in verse 19, “where the disciples were”. I think there is a correspondence between disciples and brethren. Persons who are disciples here are, I believe, those who will receive this message from the living Lord. She comes bringing word to the disciples that she had seen the Lord; that was, no doubt, the greatest thing to her, and then, that He had said these things to her.

How wonderful these things are, dear brethren. It is an immense truth that we should be of His order, “He that sanctifies and those sanctified are all of one; for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren, saying, I will declare thy name to my brethren; in the midst of the assembly will I sing thy praises”, Hebrews 2: 11, 12. I think this touches the service of God. But, if we are to know it in power, I think we must be true here, doing the will of God.

May the Lord greatly help us, not just to claim a scriptural title, and in particular this one, ‘brethren’, but rather to be exercised to be brethren characteristically; to know what it is to be true to Him, and following Him in doing the will of God, and then to have power to have our part with Him in the praise of God, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE POWER AND WISDOM OF GOD
articles.author: C. R. Byng

paragraphs.text: It is a prophetic word from previous times that God’s thoughts are higher than our thoughts, and God uses ways to secure His thoughts that are far greater than our thoughts. When the Spirit speaks of the foolishness of God and the weakness of God, He is referring to how men would take account of the wonderful ways of God. This would be seen especially in relation to the cross. “The foolishness of the preaching” was that men should preach a crucified Man as the Saviour of the world. Never was there a time when God must have seemed so foolish to men, but in fact it was the unfolding of the infinite wisdom of God, for it was the way in which God secures a world for Himself.

The righteousness of God necessitated that His rights must be honoured; His rights must always be honoured. The word of the cross involves the detailed instruction from God as to the way He has dealt in Christ with everything that stood out against the throne. As men went by the foot of the cross they said in their derision, “Let the Christ the King of Israel descend now from the cross, that we may see and may believe”, Mark 15: 32. They were really saying, ‘How foolish it is!’, but we would understand, beloved brethren, that in the cross God has dealt with every matter. The infinite wisdom of God lay behind it; as it says in 1 Corinthians 2: 7, “That hidden wisdom which God had predetermined before the ages for our glory” lay behind the coming in of Jesus to this scene.

For four thousand years man had been tried and had failed, but in the wisdom of God the ends of the ages came. When the fulness of the time was come, there came here as a Babe One who was to remove the whole lawless system and bring in what was for God. In His creation God had anticipated that men would scoff at His wisdom and He put small creatures in the creation of whom the Spirit of God can say, they are little but exceeding wise (Proverbs 30: 24). There were some wise men who came to worship Jesus as He was in the manger, but how few there were who understood that the Saviour was there. As Jesus moved amongst men in public service all the wisdom of God was there in a Man, wisdom that shone in infinite love and operated in all that He said and did. In all His parables and miracles He brought God in; as we have been taught. He brought God in and shut man out. That is the wisdom of God, which we are slow to appreciate. But the Spirit would help us to understand that what God does in a hidden way is to be enlarged in a world of His own making, what we may speak of as the third world, (see J.T. N.S. Vol. 98, p.83).

Scripture speaks of the world before the flood, the then world. We are now in this world, which is the second world. We are looking forward to the world to come, the third world, when God’s wisdom will be seen as Christ deals with all the problems of all the nations. There is going to be the fulfilment of what He said, “And I, if I be lifted up out of the earth, will draw all to me”, John 12: 32. Men are being drawn to Him at the present time in faith. In the world to come all men will see that He is the One who has in Himself the solution to every problem. The One who is going to solve the problems of the world has the solution to every problem in our lives and in all our local assemblies. How wise He is! Men marvelled at His wisdom and went away. Let us marvel and stay near Him. A queen of the south came to hear the wisdom of Solomon and she had to say the half had not been told and that “Thou exceedest the report that I heard”, 1 Kings 10: 7. Let us draw near to Christ and by experience find that His wisdom is able to deal with all our matters. No matter is too difficult for the wisdom of Christ. No matter is too small to call out His interest. No grief is too small to call out His sympathy. “The foolishness of God is wiser than men”.

Then the word says, “The weakness of God is stronger than men”. He was crucified in weakness. How weak it seemed in the eyes of men when Jesus hung on that cross of shame with one robber on one side and another robber on the other side. Where was there a greater spectacle of weakness? When He died He was laid in a tomb, but not the tomb that men had planned, for God kept every detail under control. The power of God was greater than all the power of man, and Jesus was not buried with the wicked. He was buried in a tomb that had been kept for that purpose. It was the grain of wheat falling into the ground and dying, but how much fruit there has been! He was crucified in weakness, but He lives by God’s power (2 Corinthians 13: 4), and as we are here as those who believe in Jesus, we are witnesses of the mighty power of God. We await the power that is going to transform our bodies, when the dead in Christ will rise first, and then those of us who are living are going to be changed and caught up. The power that is going to be experienced then is the power that is towards us now. The wisdom of God and the power of God go together, and they both have their source in the heart of God Himself.

As we believe in God, difficulties become a means of His showing His power. When the twelve spies came back from the land of Canaan there were ten of them marked by lack of faith. They said the difficulties were too great, they might as well give up, everything was lost. They would really say, in effect, that there will be no collective experience again as the enemies are too great. But there were two men who had faith. Joshua and Caleb had faith in God and rather than being occupied with the difficulties they said, ‘The very difficulties will be food for us’ (Numbers 14: 9), and that is the pathway of the christian. In our weakness naturally we shrink from difficulties and would like to make a diversion round them. But as we learn to know God we find that the best way is the straight way, the way of righteousness.

We find that if we are kept in the way of righteousness, instead of difficulties hindering us they just provide a fresh opportunity for God to show the power that He has. The psalmist says, “By my God have I leaped over a wall”, Psalm 18: 29. The wall was very real, but we know a God who is the God of resurrection. The very creation around us is a witness, there would be no pears on that tree outside if it were not for the God of resurrection. We have faith in the God who is able to do the impossible.

Let us have confidence that the strength of God is able to come in for us, to preserve us, even if we are few. I think the strength of God will be specially proved in localities where there may be just one sister, or perhaps one brother and one sister; as they seek to stand for God they will prove the power of the God who can do everything. Men would say that there is no more hope. When Abraham was promised a son he might well have said, ‘I am too old and my wife is too old’, but he found strength in faith. Let us find strength in faith, that God is always as good as His word, and behind His wisdom and His power there lies the infinite love of the God we know.

It is a feature of the wisdom and power of God that He waits. We find it difficult to wait, but it was a commendation of the beloved brethren in Philadelphia that the Lord said, “Thou hast kept the word of my patience”, Revelation 3: 10. The Lord Jesus has waited nearly two thousand years for His heavenly bride. The Lord is waiting patiently. Let us be restful in patience because the Lord is coming. Where we read in 2 Peter 3 the Spirit would give us an impression of the detailed knowledge of the Lord. We may think that a day comes when things are too difficult, but the Lord knows about the detailed difficulties far better than we do, because one day is spread out with Him as if it were a thousand years. He sees the detail that we see not, but then we understand that one thousand years are just as one day with the Lord. So let us be patient, beloved. How long a thousand years seems, but in the greatness of God He spans that period and it is just as one day.

Men may say that the Lord is delaying, but we are not to say that He delays His promise as some account of delay. Men usually delay because they have not the wisdom and the power to carry out what they want to do. The desire of man is to do at once what he wants to do, but God does not wait because of lack of wisdom or power, but because He is the longsuffering God, “not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance”. So if we wonder why the Lord is waiting, let us understand that His longsuffering comes into it. The long book of Job is to teach us to understand more of God, for James says of that, “Ye have heard of the endurance of Job, and seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is full of tender compassion and pitiful”, James 5: 11. If we are thinking of persons who have not yet repented, let us remember the Lord is longsuffering. Maybe He is waiting, before He proceeds with other matters, so that one person might repent and come to the knowledge of the truth.

Behind the wisdom and the power of God there lies the love that has waited on every one of us. The Lord would appeal to each of us that we might give our hearts and our lives more fully to Him than ever before. Let us yield to His desire and be strengthened in our inward longings to know what it is, like Enoch of old, to walk with God and be pleasing to Him. We shall find others to walk with, persons who with pure hearts desire to be pleasing to the Lord.

And as we think of such, we think of the Supper on the morrow, if the Lord will, when the consummation of the wisdom and the power of God will be freshly experienced. We find that out of the remembrance of One who has died there is power that transports us in spirit into a realm of life where everything is for God. May the Lord bless the word.

The tears of the saints are, and always have been, of great interest to God. So the apostle Paul is free to tell us about his tears, and what occasioned them; and he evidently valued them in others for, in writing to his child Timothy, he specifically refers to his tears—“remembering thy tears” he says, 2 Timothy 1: 4. David, too, evidently had some understanding of the value that God placed upon the tears of His people for he had liberty to ask God to put his tears into His bottle (see Psalm 56: 8).

In the present circumstances of the testimony there is much that causes our hearts sorrow, and we do not know what tears are being shed in secret. But God would graciously comfort our burdened hearts by having us realise that He is taking account of them, and the reasons for them, and would remind us that a day is coming when “he shall wipe away every tear”
(Revelation 21: 4)— every tear. How very blessed!

Whatever occasions our tears, God is assuring us that He is regarding them. He knows all that each one is passing through. Our Father—how tender are His compassions! Not a sparrow falls to the ground without Him, and Jesus adds “ye are better than many sparrows”, Matthew 10: 31. So every detail in our lives is taken account of by our Father. There are tears which arise in the sphere of natural relationships and these are acceptable in His sight. We have reached the last days when, as the scripture says, “men shall be ... without natural affection” (2 Timothy 3: 2, 3); but natural affection is of God, so the expression of grief following the death of a loved one is not without its value before Him.

But then there are the sorrows connected with the testimony of our Lord. We speak carefully, but each of us here has had, and is still having, some experience of these. So I think it would be for our strengthening to call attention to these references to the tears and weeping of the beloved apostle Paul. In this second letter to the Corinthians he discloses that he wrote the first epistle “out of much tribulation and distress of heart … with many tears”. You would not have gathered this from what he wrote but, now that it had become effective in bringing about recovery, he is free to tell them what it had cost him to write, as he did so faithfully.

But he told them this, “not that ye may be grieved, but that ye may know the love which I have very abundantly towards you”. What affection! After having “remained there a year and six months, teaching among them the word of God” (Acts 18: 11) how he must have felt the terrible disorder that had come into that assembly (see 1 Corinthians 5: 1; 11: 17–22), yet he still retained an abundant affection for them. This would help us to have right feelings towards brethren who are not going on rightly, who are still refusing to judge what is wicked.

So in the midst of our tears as to them, tears which, like the Psalmist, we are free to ask our God to put into His bottle, we would retain an attitude of affection with the longing that the day should come when it can be disclosed to some at least that we their brethren have maintained affection for them.

In speaking to the elders of the assembly at Ephesus, whom he called over to Miletus, Paul reminds them of the character of his service in that city. He says, “for three years, night and day, I ceased not admonishing each one of you with tears”. What a service! We do not wonder at the quality of the result reached. Of course the Lord was in it, and the Holy Spirit had operated in power, but the scripture records the devotion and fervent affection of this beloved servant, his tears entering into it, in the detailed service of admonishing each one of them.
And now he warns them of what will come, in grievous wolves—and that from among their own selves men should rise up speaking perverted things to draw away disciples after them.

Have we not witnessed this in recent years? It is no new thing in assembly history. But Paul is going on and he commits them to God and to the word of His grace. And the Spirit is strengthening us to go on, even if it involves tears. Each of us needs constant adjustment and the service of admonishing; we are exhorted to do this—in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, yes, (see Colossians 3: 16)—but the service may require tears; so let us, as strengthened by the Spirit, follow the example of the apostle. It is “night and day”, the day is before us; “at even weeping cometh for the night, and at morn there is rejoicing”, Psalm 30: 5. We know that the morning of rejoicing is very near. Indeed we shall anticipate it on the morrow as we assemble to celebrate the Lord’s supper and have part in the service of God in the assembly, for in the Spirit’s power we are released from the sorrows of the testimony to enjoy what is our eternal portion.

The saints in Philippi, in the way they continued in support of the gospel, were a cause of joy to the apostle but he tells them about some—he says, “and now tell you even weeping”—who are enemies of the cross of Christ and mind earthly things. I suppose they were persons who had a place in some assemblies but were merely professing christians. This is another thing that saddens our hearts at the present time, and the apostle helps us to have right feelings as to such. No true believer should be an enemy of the cross of Christ; so let us see to it that we are thoroughly in accord with the cross and what it means as separating us from the world and all that is in it. And let us not fall into the snare of minding earthly things for our minds are to be on what is heavenly—“have your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth”, Colossians 3: 2.

Paul here presents himself and others, as a model which we are to imitate. He does not hesitate to tell us about his tears and his weeping and it is in order that we might follow his example. So the shedding of tears in relation to our experiences in the pathway of the testimony is nothing to be ashamed of—it is recorded seven times of Joseph that he wept, and of Moses as a babe that he wept—and God would assure us that He takes perfect account of such tears and we can be free to ask Him to put them into His bottle. Then there are the compensating joys; within a few verses Paul is saying, “Rejoice in the Lord always—again I will say, Rejoice”, Philippians 4: 4. So, in the midst of the sorrows and the joys, may we be strengthened to go on in faithfulness to the Lord, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: LOOKING UP
articles.author: A. R. Stevens
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: I think, brethren, we would all agree that running alongside of obedience is the thought of dependence. It is a quality that is very pleasurable to God. It was seen in perfection in our Lord Jesus Christ, who we know was God manifest in flesh. One of the great purposes of the Lord taking the condition of manhood was to show men how they should live for the pleasure of God. So the quality of dependence was seen in perfection in that blessed One.

My impression is that God is teaching us through circumstances to be dependent persons. I think the circumstances in which we are found, assembly-wise particularly, are ordered of God in view of teaching us to be dependent. You take an occasion like this—most of us are just feeble persons, not rightly able to fill out the idea of what is prophetic, but as found in the spirit of dependence and cast upon God. He brings in a word to encourage us and to stimulate us so that the character of manhood that was seen in Christ might mark us. This, we know, is God’s great thought for us.

As we come on to the end of the dispensation, God in His great love and grace is using circumstances to teach us. I remember, as a young man, when I first came among brethren, I heard the older brethren speak of the ministry of circumstances,

and I think God is largely reaching His and that way. We can hardly understand the present time in which we are found; a time in which what we were accustomed to and recognised as being strong and reliable, has now become, outwardly, a splintered condition. Yet, as we have often been reminded, God’s thoughts have not changed; He is the same God; His plans have not changed; His love is unchanged, and He is going through to completion with all that He ever had in mind. But God is bent on teaching us, through circumstances, to be dependent persons.

We see the idea of dependence in the portion of the Psalm we have read. I am not saying that this is all that is meant, but I think it enters into the thought of looking up. The psalmist was not self-centred, he is not engaged with his own circumstances at this point, but is prepared to address God and look up. Let us look up, dear brethren. As we look up we find that God is a great encourager of His people. As we look abroad in the world circumstances are distressing; but as we look up we get our eyes on an order of things which is perfectly intact.

The psalmist would have this in his heart. He learned it through experience—it is a psalm of David. David was one who had outstanding experience with God. So he says, “Jehovah, in the morning shalt thou hear my voice; in the morning will I address myself to thee, and will look up”.
May we be encouraged to look up and be marked increasingly by this wonderful spirit of dependence. May it be so for His name’s sake.

In Luke the Lord’s teaching would show that if we have temporal things, we are to use them in view of the future. The world uses money in view of the present, to add to self here; whereas, the “unjust steward” used what came to his hand in view of the future; the Lord using what he did to teach us to use temporal things in relation to what is eternal. Luke speaks much of money, especially after chapter 15.

Let each challenge his own heart—Did I ever influence a person on the principle of holy love? As soon as you begin to influence on this principle, you begin to rule on the principle of the twelve thrones and you are ruling twelve tribes. They are intact, they refer to the saints, I understand, as available to heaven, amenable to the influence of heaven, but that influence exerted through persons. Each christian has it within his range to influence another and another and another; the wider his range the more distinguished his throne … Would that I could set the brethren in movement! The very youngest can begin with influencing another, his sister or brother, or even his parents—I have known of this influencing another in love. How fitting is the throne of Christ’s glory in the midst of those twelve thrones!

Why did the Lord not leave the children of Israel in Egypt? Why did He not enlighten them by Moses, and let them stay there, in order that they might enlighten the Egyptians? ... God never intended to make a slave an evangelist ... If you are to convey glad tidings from God, you must be a free man. The message is too great to entrust to a slave. God thinks too much of the glad tidings to entrust them to a slave. They are too magnificent. The gospel is the grandest thing God has ever presented. You cannot overestimate the gospel, and the more you understand it, the more you will see that the Son only could be the Bearer of it to man.
‘ I AM A VOICE’—When John was approached flatteringly by the Jews—“Art thou Elias? …

Art thou the prophet?”, his simple answer was, “No … I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness. Make straight the path of the Lord”, John 1: 22, 23. It was not only what John said; his whole manner of life was a voice, calling attention to Jesus, making way for Him, and showing that John thought so little of himself and so much of Christ; as he said, “He must increase, but I must decrease”, John 3; 30. Each of our lives has a voice. Our habits, our interests, our dress, our speech, all have a voice. They proclaim either that I have myself before me, or that, like John, I prefer Christ. Let our whole manner of life be such as to show that we are lovers of Jesus. Thus He will be drawn attention to.
